source: Kidd, Piantadosi, Aslin (2012) The Goldilocks Effect: infants attend to sequences neither too simple nor too complex
finding: 7 to 8 month old infants looked away most from events that an ideal-learner model rated as very predictable or very surprising. Look-away followed a U shape against model complexity.
numbers: Exp 1: 42 infants analysed (44 tested, mean 7.9 months), single-box display; Goldilocks complexity about 1.25 bits. Exp 2: 30 infants (mean 7.6 months), three-box display, 32 sequences. Cox regression: only squared complexity significant in Exp 1; U shape also held for the transitional model in Exp 2.
quote: infants implicitly seek to maintain intermediate rates of information absorption
limits: Authors call the effect relatively small. Complexity comes from the authors' own Dirichlet-multinomial model, a linking assumption. Look-away is a proxy for interest. Small samples; no exact odds ratio recovered from the text.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that attention is best at intermediate surprise, not at maximum surprise. It supports ranking by learnable surprise, but it is about error level, not error change.

source: Poli, Serino, Mars, Hunnius (2020) Infants tailor their attention to maximize learning, Science Advances 6:eabb5053
finding: Infants' looking away was best predicted by the learning progress (information gain) of the trial, more than by surprise or predictability. Looking time on targets rose with the amount of model updating.
numbers: 50 infants recruited, 43 analysed (mean 7 m 29 d); 16 sequences (4 deterministic, 12 probabilistic) of cue-target trials with 4 locations. Generalized additive model: learning progress Wald chi2=48.87, edf=4, P<0.001; surprise chi2=19.38, P<0.001; predictability chi2=21.87, P<0.001. Surprise and predictability effects were about 3 and 5 times weaker than learning progress.
limits: One lab, one task, one age group, no replication found. Learning progress is computed from an ideal-learner model chosen by the authors; infants are assumed to match it. Surprise and predictability were unrelated to looking time on targets.
agent_relevance: Best human support for learning progress as the selection signal. Suggests a progress ranker should beat a pure error ranker, but the human data is a toy visual task, not problem choice.

source: Kidd, Piantadosi, Aslin (2014) The Goldilocks effect in infant auditory attention, Child Development
finding: Same group extends the Goldilocks pattern to auditory sequences (listing only; full text not opened because the full-text server returned an error).
numbers: Europe PMC lists 105 citations. No N or effect size verified.
limits: Snippet-level only; same authors, so not an independent replication. No independent replication of Kidd 2012 was located in this search.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays partly open: the visual result is extended by its own authors, not independently replicated.

source: Oudeyer, Kaplan, Hafner (2007) Intrinsic Motivation Systems for Autonomous Mental Development, IEEE TEVC 11(2)
finding: Intelligent Adaptive Curiosity (IAC) picks actions whose expected error decrease is largest. In a sensorimotor simulation the agent moved through stages: random actions, then an easy learnable zone, then a harder zone, avoiding a zone with nothing to learn. This is the journal form of the Kaplan and Oudeyer 2004 learning-progress idea.
numbers: Simulation, 5000 steps: after the first 250 steps the robot focuses on the first learnable zone; at about 3000 actions IAC shifts to the next zone and then spends 85% of its time there (15% random action). RANDOM has 33% of examples in the easy zone. IAC prediction error reaches a plateau near 5000 actions at mean error about 0.09 and goes below RANDOM. MAX (pick highest error) is the built-in error-only control.
limits: Numbers read from text and figure captions; the Kaplan and Oudeyer 2004 paper itself could not be fetched. Toy simulation, one agent. Regions are found by the algorithm's own splitting.
agent_relevance: Founding result for gap 4: progress-driven choice shows ordered stages, avoids the unlearnable zone and beats random on the zone of interest.

source: Oudeyer, Kaplan, Hafner (2007) AIBO play-mat experiment and 200 simulated runs
finding: A real Sony AIBO on a play mat self-organised developmental sequences with IAC. A simulated world built from robot data was run 200 times to count how often structured trajectories appear.
numbers: 200 simulated runs: the structured trajectory (measure 2) appears in 34% of runs; 100% of runs reach a period of repeatedly biting the biteable object; 78% reach repeated bashing; focused bite appears before focused bash in the large majority of runs.
limits: Sequences are defined by the authors' own peak-pattern measures; the physical run is a case study. No comparison against other exploration rules in this experiment.
agent_relevance: A progress signal gives structured but not uniform curricula: only about a third of runs follow the cleanest order. Expect variance in an LLM version.

source: Schmidhuber (2010) Formal Theory of Creativity, Fun, and Intrinsic Motivation (1990-2010), IEEE TAMD
finding: Review of the 1991 to 2002 curiosity systems. The 1991 error-based reward drives the agent to high-error places, which fails under noise; the fix is reward for predictor improvement. Experiments are described only as showing advantages over random exploration; no numbers are given.
numbers: No quantitative results in the review for the 1991 or 1995 systems. 1991 first system: reward proportional to predictor error. 1991 Adaptive Curiosity variant: a model of the predictor's improvement (MSE change) gives the reward. 1995: reward is the KL distance between predictor beliefs before and after an observation.
quote: Experiments illustrate the advantages of this type of directed, curious exploration over traditional random exploration.
limits: Self-review by the originator. He says the 1991 AC system handles noise because noisy targets give no measurable learning progress; this is a design argument, not a measurement. He also disputes Oudeyer's claim that IAC is better suited to stochastic worlds.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answer: the 1991 paper has no benchmark numbers to recover. Treat it as a design precedent, not as an effect size.

source: Hou, An, Du (2025/2026) Beyond Noisy-TVs: Noise-Robust Exploration via Learning Progress Monitoring (LPM)
finding: A learning-progress reward (dual network) was tested against ICM, Ensemble, RND, AMA, EME and EDT in one code base on Noisy MNIST, MiniWorld, MountainCar and Atari. It kept working when noise was added while baselines degraded.
numbers: MiniWorld 3D maze (2,176 visitable states), 10 seeds: LPM mean 1,347.6 visited states, 95.3 above the second best; best deterministic was EDT at 1276.1; LPM best under state noise (1434.0) and action noise (1340.0). Atari with CIFAR-10 noise action: LPM drop 3.9% (Space Invaders), 4.7% (UpNDown), +0.3% (Ms PacMan); EME fell 100%. LPM best in 4 of 6 games, 128 seeds.
limits: Authors' own method, single group (v2 April 2026). MountainCar Table 2 values did not survive text extraction; only the 12.4% LPM drop is stated. Noise is artificial.
agent_relevance: Closest to gap 7: a same-benchmark head-to-head of progress vs error (ICM, RND, ensemble). Progress wins mainly under noise; on the clean maze EDT was best.

source: Hou, An, Du (2025/2026) LPM on Montezuma's Revenge and Noisy MNIST
finding: On Montezuma's Revenge LPM got non-trivial score within 20M exploration steps while RND needed 50M. NGU (re-implemented) got no extrinsic reward in 50M steps. On Noisy MNIST LPM rewards deterministic and stochastic transitions alike and goes to zero fast; AMA and EDT keep favouring stochastic transitions longer.
numbers: Montezuma: LPM non-trivial at 20M steps vs RND 50M; NGU 0 at 50M. Noisy MNIST: 5 runs.
limits: NGU is the authors' own re-implementation. Montezuma is shown in a figure with no scalar in the text. Few seeds on Noisy MNIST.
agent_relevance: Progress signal can also help on clean sparse tasks, but this is one paper.

source: Gradient-Momentum Coupling (2026) A parameter-space proxy for learning progress
finding: A progress proxy based on gradient times momentum keeps allocation near uniform across noisy task groups while prediction error chases the noisiest. Swapped into ICM it recovers exploration lost to unpredictable observations on four MiniGrid MultiRoom tasks.
numbers: 20 seeds with 95% CI in controlled CIFAR-10 and MNIST experiments; four MiniGrid MultiRoom tasks. Scalar tables lost in text extraction.
limits: Preprint, one group. The main controlled experiments are supervised classification, not agents. Slight bias against the no-noise group after saturation.
agent_relevance: A second source, independent of d07, that error chases noise and progress does not. Supports K02 and K03; still not a scaffold test.

source: Dai et al. (2025) CDE: Curiosity-Driven Exploration for LLM RLVR, arXiv 2509.09675 (ICLR 2026)
finding: Perplexity bonus on the actor and multi-head critic variance bonus add a modest gain over GRPO and PPO on math. Only one base model is used.
numbers: All runs use Qwen3-4B-Base with Verl. GRPO: average 48.2, AIME24 Avg@16 20.8, AIME25 Avg@16 21.0, MATH 87.3. GRPO + PPL bonus: average 50.6, AIME24 23.3, AIME25 23.5, MATH 87.7. PPO: AIME24 17.8, average 46.5; PPO + bonus AIME24 18.3. The bonus weight must decay; staircase schedule was best.
limits: Single base model, single codebase; no Llama or other family. No replication of CDE itself by others found. Gains are 1 to 3 points.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: CDE itself is not replicated. It is training-time and not usable in a prompt-only scaffold.

source: Gao et al. (2025) IMAGINE: Navigate the Unknown, intrinsic-motivation guided exploration for LLM RLVR, arXiv 2505.17621
finding: A different sequence-level intrinsic reward applied after advantage computation improves PPO, GRPO and DAPO on four datasets and two base models, with larger gains on harder tasks.
numbers: GRPO to IMAGINE(GRPO), Qwen2.5-3B: GSM8K 0.8082 to 0.8251 (+2.09%); Countdown-34 0.6711 to 0.7132 (+6.27%); Countdown-4 0.3872 to 0.4739 (+22.39%). PPO Countdown-4 0.3307 to 0.3812. Size scan on Countdown-34: 0.5B 0.0033 to 0.0107; 1.5B 0.4532 to 0.5068. Abstract: +22.23% on AIME 2024. Base models Qwen2.5-3B and DeepSeek-7B.
limits: Not a replication of CDE; a separate method with the same aim. Few seeds (std reported); gains largest where the baseline is lowest.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: curiosity-like bonuses for RLVR help on at least two base families, but the claim is that similar methods work, not that CDE replicates.

source: Prioritized Generative Replay (2025, ICLR) third-party DMLab table with ECO baseline
finding: A different group ran PPO, PPO with curiosity, PPO with RND and PPO with ECO on the randomized (noisy-TV) DMLab maze, 10 seeds, 10M steps.
numbers: Table 5, average returns: PPO 7.3 +/-2.7 (Sparse) and 4.1 +/-2.4 (Very Sparse); PPO+RND 16.3 +/-3.6 and 12.9 +/-1.9; PGR(ECO) 21.9 +/-2.6. ECO row values are hard to align in the extracted table (5.7 +/-2.2 and 8.0 +/-1.8 appear near it).
limits: Table layout garbled by PDF extraction; the PPO+ECO cell is not confirmed. A web-search summary had attributed 16.3 to ECO, which the table does not support (16.3 sits on the RND row). Not clear that official ECO code was used.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: only partial. ECO appears as a baseline outside its authors, but there is no clean replication of the 40.5 DMLab number and no text transfer.

source: Binder et al. (2025) Looking Inward: Language models can learn about themselves by introspection (ICLR 2025)
finding: After finetuning, a model predicts properties of its own behavior better than a second model trained on its behavior, and its self-predictions are better calibrated. Untrained models are weak at it.
numbers: Llama 70B predicts itself 48.5% vs GPT-4o predicting Llama 70B 31.8%; GPT-4o predicts itself 49.4% vs Llama 70B 36.6%; Llama 70B vs GPT-4o gap +17%. GPT-3.5 advantage only +0.8%. Calibration mean absolute deviation: untrained 23.0, self-trained 8.7, cross-trained 21.3. After a behaviour change GPT-4o predicts the new behaviour 35.4% vs old 21.7% (as reported by the search summary, not re-read).
limits: Requires finetuning on self-prediction; simple short-output tasks only; fails on long outputs such as stories. Not a prompt-only test. Baseline is guessing the most common answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a verbal self-prediction signal exists but is weak without training and limited to short outputs. A scaffold that stores a stated expectation should expect noisy, poorly calibrated surprise.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking: are reasoning models losing critical thinking skill?
finding: Reasoning models spend far more tokens on questions whose key premise was removed, cannot abstain, and keep thinking even after noticing the gap. Non-reasoning models answer short.
numbers: Per the paper's summary: about 2x to 4x more tokens on missing-premise questions than on well-defined ones; DeepSeek-R1 produced thousands of tokens on an undefined-variable query. Datasets: rule-based formulas, SVAMP, GSM8K, MATH500 variants.
limits: Exact per-model table not recorded; the 2 to 4x ratio comes from the paper's summary, not my own table read. Reasoning LLMs, not scaffolds with a budget rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: nearest real noisy-TV for LLMs. Unanswerable questions pull tokens. A scaffold needs an explicit stop rule when error does not fall.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring beyond curiosity rewards: language-driven exploration in RL
finding: Language-driven exploration claims better sample efficiency than curiosity rewards on BabyAI-Text, MiniHack, Atari and Crafter (snippet only).
limits: Search snippet only; not opened. Cost of LLM calls not verified.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open; nothing here is verified.

source: Search negative result: LLM scaffolds with learning-progress ranking, noisy-TV traps, token accounting (this run)
finding: In 8 WebSearch calls plus arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar attempts (the APIs returned HTTP 429 for most calls), no paper was found that (a) compares a learning-progress ranker with an error or novelty ranker for subproblem choice in a prompt-only LLM agent at equal tokens, (b) tests noisy-TV traps in an LLM scaffold, or (c) accounts for tokens spent by curiosity operators.
numbers: MAGELLAN (c01) remains the closest: LP-based goal choice with a trained LLM, 80% impossible goals in Little-Zoo.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search budget; forward-citation lists for ECO, MAGELLAN and OMNI could not be pulled. The last WebSearch was refused (shared budget used up).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 3, 8 and 10 should be treated as open questions and as tests the agent project could run itself.
